divisions.question: Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013 - Consideration in Detail - Workplace bullying
Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013 — Consideration in Detail — Right of entry

Eric Abetz The Senate is debating the latest instalment of the 400 pages of amendments to Labor's so-called perfect Fair Work laws. Remember the laws that were so good they were sacrosanct? The right balance had been achieved! No change was needed! Well, here we are, 400 pages of amendments later, in circumstances where Labor have previously said that there should be no change, especially before an election. Indeed, whilst Labor themselves were in government, way back when they actually had principled ministers and a principled government, right back when they used to know what they believed in, they were concerned to ensure that a genuinely right balance was achieved in workplace relations law, when they were about reform, and when they were about the national interest. They had a Minister for Industrial Relations, one Ralph Willis, who in 1987 said: The government has decided not to go ahead with the industrial relations bill this session. The legislation will not be debated and will be left to lie on the table. There is already a large measure of agreement between employer groups, the union movement and the government on the legislation, but some significant differences remain. This government has constantly pursued a process of consultation rather than confrontation. Because of the remaining differences of view over the legislation, the government will have discussions … That was the principled stand way back in 1987. Isn't it a pity that the current Minister for Workplace Relations, the man who thinks the job of Minister for Workplace Relations is simply that of an upmarket trade union boss, cannot show us the same sort of integrity, the same sort of commitment to the national interest. That was Mr Willis all those years ago. Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013 - Second Reading - Workplace Bullying
Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013 - Second Reading - Right of entry

speeches.speaker: Anne McEwen
speeches.brief: The Selection of Bills Committee presented its fourth report of 2013, recommending 18 bills be referred to various Senate committees for inquiry and report by specific dates, and that certain other bills not be referred.

speeches.speaker: Sussan Ley
speeches.brief: Criticised the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013 for ignoring the bulk of its own review's 53 recommendations while expanding union right of entry, noting the government spent more than $160,000 intervening in the Barclay v Bendigo TAFE case on the side of union officials, and that union membership has fallen to about 13 or 15 per cent of the workforce.

speeches.speaker: Amanda Rishworth
speeches.brief: Defended the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013's expansion of flexible work rights for carers and domestic violence victims, its extension of concurrent parental leave from three weeks to eight weeks, and its new anti-bullying powers for the Fair Work Commission backed by $21.4 million over four years, honouring the advocacy of Brodie Panlock's parents after Panlock's death.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: Argued the Fair Work Amendment Bill's right-of-entry changes would let unions default to meeting workers in lunchrooms even though only 13 per cent of employees are union members, and cited CFMEU official Joe McDonald's history of criminal charges and more than $1 million in union fines since 2005.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Argued the Fair Work Amendment Bill exists to reward the union movement, noting only 12 per cent of private sector workers are union members while the government's cabinet includes several former union officials, including ministers previously with the Australian Workers' Union and the Liquor, Hospitality and Miscellaneous Union.

speeches.speaker: Richard Marles
speeches.brief: Defended the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013's four reforms covering family-friendly leave, anti-bullying powers, right of entry and penalty rates, citing a Productivity Commission estimate that workplace bullying costs the economy up to $36 billion a year, and said productivity is now three times higher than under Work Choices.

speeches.speaker: Karen Andrews
speeches.brief: Criticised the government for rushing the Fair Work Amendment Bill through parliament before the House committee's report on its 41 submissions was tabled, citing opposition from the Australian Industry Group and the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, both of which said the bill was unbalanced and lacked a regulatory impact statement.

speeches.speaker: Scott Buchholz
speeches.brief: Opposed the Fair Work Amendment Bill despite supporting over 87.3 per cent of the government's other legislation, arguing its right-of-entry demands go too far for small business, drawing on his experience employing more than 100 staff across 14 depots in Queensland.

speeches.speaker: Scott Buchholz
speeches.brief: Criticised the Fair Work Amendment Bill for lacking a regulatory impact statement, noted amendments to the Fair Work Act since 2009 now total more than 400 pages including 157 new or extended union rights identified by the Australian Industry Group, and said the government spent more than $160,000 intervening on the union side in the Barclay High Court case.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: Said the Greens would support the Fair Work Amendment Bill while moving amendments to strengthen it, citing that one in four Australian employees has no sick leave and that Australia has the second-highest use of temporary workforce in the OECD after Spain, and pointed to Qantas's 2011 fleet grounding as an example of employers using tactical industrial action to force arbitration.

speeches.speaker: Josh Frydenberg
speeches.brief: Noted that before the last election the Greens received $325,000 from the Victorian branch of the Electrical Trade Union, with $125,000 going to the member for Melbourne's campaign and $200,000 to Senator Richard Di Natale.

speeches.speaker: Josh Frydenberg
speeches.brief: Argued the Fair Work Amendment Bill panders to unions, noting the union movement represents only 13 per cent of the private sector workforce yet controls 50 per cent of Labor conference votes, cited reports the Australian Workers' Union made 156 site visits to BHP's Worsley aluminium site in 2012 and more than 200 visits to the Pluto project in its first 90 days, and said the coalition delivered 22 per cent real wage growth in government.

speeches.speaker: Jamie Briggs
speeches.brief: Opposed the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013, arguing it protects union power and existing job holders rather than helping the unemployed find work, and contrasted it with the coalition's preference for reducing workplace regulation to create more employment opportunities.

speeches.speaker: Rowan Ramsey
speeches.brief: Debated the Fair Work Amendment Bill, welcoming the government's withdrawal of contested right-of-entry clauses, and recalled a parliamentary inquiry into workplace bullying that received 319 submissions and made 23 recommendations, noting the bill implements only recommendation 23 on an individual right of recourse for bullied workers.

speeches.speaker: Bill Shorten
speeches.brief: Defended the Fair Work Amendment Bill's family-friendly and right-of-entry provisions, accused the opposition of spreading a false 'joy-ride scheme' claim about union officials, and confirmed the bill's new bullying jurisdiction would commence on 1 January 2014, citing seven consecutive quarters of productivity growth under Labor.

speeches.speaker: Sussan Ley
speeches.brief: Responded that the coalition supports these particular amendments to the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013 as recommendations of the Fair Work Commission broadly backed by industry, while making clear it disagrees with the rest of the bill.

speeches.speaker: Bill Shorten
speeches.brief: Presented a supplementary explanatory memorandum to the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013 and moved a government amendment clarifying that Schedule 3's provisions will commence on 1 January 2014 rather than on proclamation or up to six months after royal assent, to provide certainty to employers and employees.

speeches.speaker: Sussan Ley
speeches.brief: Moved amendments removing expanded union right-of-entry provisions, arguing the government had withdrawn an agreement at the last minute and that existing rights already allowed excessive workplace access; debate was interrupted.

speeches.speaker: Scott Buchholz
speeches.brief: Warned that the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2013 could have unintended consequences for family businesses and larger enterprises by enabling union representatives to seek access to lunchrooms, despite businesses providing free on-site meeting space.
